Report of the 
Chairman of the 
Board of the 
Montreal YMCA, 
Mr. Claude Lemay 


In September 1989, the Montreal 
YMCA initiated the second phase of 
its strategic-planning process from 
which two major themes evolved 
after some collective reflections. 
Firstly, we need to consolidate our 
operations after a period of major 
capital investments which were 
made to better serve our constituen- 
cy. Secondly, given that we want to 
serve the entire population of greater 
Montreal, it was clearly stated that 
the YMCA has to become active and 
present in new areas. 


Therefore, a team of volunteers and 
staff were asked to analyse the 
programming of the YMCA, the 
expansion and consolidation of its 
operations, the development of its 
human resources as well as the 
financial situation of the organization. 
The work which they accomplished 
was exceptional. It was also decided 
that the strategic-planning process 
would extend over a period of five 
years. Moreover, given the length of 
time required to put the finishing 
touches to the strategies so far de- 
veloped for the buildings of both the 
Downtown YMCA and Kamp 
Kanawana, as well as for the Du Parc 
YMCA, the available financial 
resources for the new activities 
recommended in the study will 
constantly be reevaluated. 


The Montreal YMCA, a unique 
organization, draws its energy from 
its history and experience, its faith in 


the potential of the individual, its 
partnership between volunteers and 
staff, as well as its direct ties with 
the needs and aspirations of the 
citizens and communities it serves. 
Our Association is indeed a dynamic 
social entrepreneur and an educator 
that is continually seeking to estab- 
lish an equilibrium between its social 
relevance and financial viability. This 
considerable challenge characterizes 
well the year that is coming to a 
close and | am pleased to underline 
both the personal and professional 
commitment which has been shown 
by all our volunteers and staff. 


A heartfelt thanks to each and 
everyone of you. 


Mr. Claude 
Lemay (4th from 
the left) with 
members of the 
Saint-Laurent 
Senior Citizens 
Neighborhood 
Association at 
the Saint-Laurent 
YMCA. 


Me Claude Lemay 


YMCA 
On y Va! 


Report of the 
Director General of 
the Montreal YMCA, 


Mr. Solomon Kasimer 


The 1989-90 fiscal year is ending with 
the development of a Strategic Plan 
for the consolidation and expansion of 
the operations of the Association. In 
order to be in a better position to con- 
tinue to serve its community, the 
Montreal YMCA conducted an inten- 
sive study of its constituency and 
from it was able to define both the 
social and economic factors which 
characterize the Montreal metro- 
politan region. The analysis high- 
lighted the increase in poverty rates, 
the growing abuse among young 
people and the isolation of many new 
cultural communities. 


Thanks to its programs and services, 
the Montreal YMCA reached over 
150,000 people and was able to 
count on the personal and profes- 
sional support of some 3,500 volun- 
teers. Team spirit and a desire to 
better serve the community produced 
a dynamic effect through which 
everyone, volunteers and staff, 
helped us realize our social mission 
on a day-to-day basis. 


The 1989-90 fiscal year held some 
major financial challenges for the 
Association. In fact, the purchase of 
a downtown building, on the one 
hand, guaranteed us all the room we 
needed to manoeuvre as regards the 
reorganization of the Downtown 


branch; however, on the other hand, 
this purchase created a significant 
short-term debt for the Montreal 
YMCA. Our strategic-planning 
process took this new reality into 
account and as a result it was clearly 
stated that the money acquired by the 
sale of certain assets would be com- 
mitted to ensure the presence of the 
YMCA in the downtown area, 
eliminate our debt and create an 
endowment fund. 


The management of the Montreal 
YMCA is committed to the 
development of programs and 
services that meet the needs of all 
Montrealers as we enter the 
challenges of the 90's 


| would like to take this opportunity to 
personally thank all staff members 
and volunteers for their support and 
true commitment to our organization. 


Mr. Sol Kasimer 
with children 
from the 
Downtown day 
care centre. 


2h See 


Mr. Solomon Kasimer 


A Gigantic 
Pyramid 


Like a gigantic pyramid, the Montreal 
YMCA brings together over 3,500 
volunteers and close to 325 full-time 
and 1,000 part-time employees who 
work in seventeen different commu- 
nity centers and establishments 
throughout Greater Montreal. Over 
150,000 individuals participate in 
programs and benefit from services 
offered by the YMCA. 


Personal 
Development 


Eight Montreal YMCA community 
centers offer fully-equipped facilities: 
pool, gymnasium, dance studio, 
weight-training room, classrooms, 
child care space, community meeting 
rooms and mixed-use spaces. 


Downtown YMCA 


In April 1990, over 800 runners gladly 
participated in the 11th edition of the 
Bill Lewis Spring Race. This year, the 
branch reconfirmed its social role in 
the Centre-Sud community of 
Montreal with the opening of a drop- 
in baby-sitting service for single- 
parent families, its participation in the 
inauguration of two rooming houses 
for the rooming and homeless pop- 
ulation of this neighborhood, the 
creation of two newsletters (la Criée 
of Alerte Centre-Sud and I'Info-Toit), 
as well as the organization of training 
sessions for rooming-house tenants. 
Within its own walls, the branch 
welcomed a large number of partici- 
pants in its language courses and its 
programming for young children 
served both working parents and 
single parents well. Over the year, its 
residence housed a large number of 
refugees, in addition to welcoming 
travellers from outside Montreal. 


Guy-Favreau YMCA 


The Guy-Favreau YMCA has 2,500 
members. In 1989-1990, a number of 
new groups of people were added to 
the list of those who have free access 
to its facilities: handicapped persons, 
seniors from long-term care hospitals, 
children from nearby daycares and 
members of the Chinese community. 


This year, the Guy-Favreau YMCA 
was bestowed the "Meérite Kino 
Régional" award for its outstanding 
efforts in promoting physical activity. 


Hochelaga-Maisonneuve YMCA 


This year, the Hochelaga-Maisonneuve 
YMCA cooperated in the implementa- 
tion of a housing committee in the 
area, where 85% of the people are 
tenants. In addition, the setting-up of 
a C.J.S. (Coopérative jeunesse de 
services - a youth services coop- 
erative) allowed youth between 12 
and 17 years of age to create their 
own jobs and operate a cooperative 
company. The centre welcomed over 
600 children in its specialized day 
camp and 1,200 students were able 
to attend language courses, which 
represents double the amount of 
participants in these courses as 
compared to 1988-89! In accordance 
with its accessibility policy, the 
Hochelaga-Maisonneuve YMCA sub- 
sidized over 250 individuals who 
participated in its programs over 

the year. 


Notre-Dame-de-Grace YMCA 


In addition to its regular programming, 
this year the N.D.G. YMCA, in collabo- 
ration with the National Council of 
YMCAs of Ireland, took on the role of 
host branch for 14 Irish youth from 
Belfast who came to Montreal for a 
six-month stay. This inte-YMCA 
partnership allowed them to work in 
Montreal and enjoy a unique experi- 
ence in a totally different social and 
cultural context from their own. The 
local N.D.G. community as well as 
various community groups in the area 
supported this ambitious project. 
Their efforts and commitment made it 
a tremendous success. 


The YMCA, 
a family centre. 


The YMCA, 
a halfway house. 


Pointe-Saint-Charles YMCA 


The Pointe-Saint-Charles branch 
added a psycho-social element to its 
afterschool program, which on a 
weekly basis welcomes some fifty or 
so children between 6 and 12 years 
of age. Thanks to financial assis- 
tance it receives from the Conseil 
régional du centre des services 
sociaux du Montréal métropolitain 
(C.R.C.S.S.M.M.) and support from 
Ville-Marie Social Services, all pro- 
gram educators will receive training 
enabling them to deal with serious 
behaviour problems which some of 
these young people experience. As 
needed, professional social workers 
will be available to counsel both the 
youth and the educators. 


Our regular programming also re- 
sponded to the needs of seniors in 
the neighborhood, as they partici- 
pated in the Aquafitness and Stretch 
and Strength programs. 


Saint-Laurent YMCA 


The Saint-Laurent YMCA intensified 
its presence within the neighbor- 
hood. Whether through speeches 
made at the Saint-Laurent Chamber 
of Commerce, active participation in 
the creation of the Saint-Laurent 
Lions Club, the drop-in baby-sitting 
service offered at the Place Vertu 
shopping centre, or through the 
launching of its "Friendship Has No 
Age Limit" campaign, the YMCA 
answered the daily needs of its 
community while making its pro- 
grams and services accessible to 
everyone. The Saint-Laurent YMCA 
also introduced an integrated swim- 
ming and aerobic dance program for 
handicapped persons. 


Westmount YMCA 


Over one hundred volunteer instruc- 
tors received training in order to 
prepare them to lead physical 
education classes. Close to 2,500 
members benefit from personalized 
programming which allows both the 
young and not-so-young to train as a 
family. The branch also welcomed 
over 800 neighborhood school 
children for an afternoon at the Y. 


West Island YMCA Family Centre 


The partnership which ties 200 
volunteers to the staff members 
contributed to the personal develop- 
ment of some 5,000 members, chil- 
dren, adolescents and adults. All our 
physical education courses are now 
taught by a team of 112 volunteers! 
Also, it should be noted that 350 
families from within the community 
benefited from subsidies for their 
annual family memberships. 


Community 
Development 


Our community-development pro- 
grams aim for the development of 
self-reliance among citizens as 
regards the improvement of their 
quality of life. Various programs and 
services of the branch are related to 
four major social themes, namely 
employment and economic develop- 
ment, community justice initiatives, 
ethnic minority rights and urban 
development. 


Youth Enterprise Centre (Y.E.C.) 
and Job Generation 


In 1989-90, these two Montreal 
YMCA programs continued to score 
points and ensure the right to emp- 
loyment for young people. 


As a business incubator, the Y.E.C., 
assisted young entrepreneurs as 
they started up over 70 new busi- 
nesses, which created more than 
160 new jobs. |n turn, Job Gene- 
ration helped several hundreds of 
young disadvantaged people from 
different ethnocultural communities 
to find work and trained them on 
how to find and keep a job. In fact, 
75 to 80% of participants succeeded 
in finding work or returned to school. 


Compensatory Work 
Program (C. W. P.) 


Overseen by the ministére de la 
Sécurité publique, the Compensatory 
Work Program of the Montreal 
YMCA helps those who cannot pay 
their fines avoid being incarcerated, 
by allowing them to do non-remu- 
nerated work for a non-profit orga- 
nization. In 1989-90, over 3,200 
dossiers were handled by the 
counsellors of the program. Statis- 
tics confirm that 61.1% of individuals 
who were referred to the program 
successfully completed the commu- 
nity work which was assigned to 
them. The C.W.P. works in collabo- 
ration with 260 participating orga- 
nizations which, this year, benefited 
from approximately 70,000 man- 
hours of volunteer work. This 
program has already been in 
existence since 1984. 


Community Residential 
Centre (C. R. C.) 


In collaboration with the Office of the 
Solicitor General of Canada, the 
YMCA implemented a C.R.C. whose 
aim is to reintegrate into society ex- 
offenders, who come from federal 
institutions. To date, the centre has 
welcomed 82 residents; among the 
67 who completed their term, 56 
were able to find employment. 


In addition, the Entre-Temps Program 
offers specialized services for ex- 
offenders who come from provincial 
institutions. 70% of these residents 
also succeeded in finding work, 
which gave them the opportunity to 
reintegrate into society. Finally, a 
third program, SEMO (an external 
manpower service) has been working 
in this same field since 1981! 


West Island Community Centre 


Through proven programs, this West 
Island centre reaches out to young 
people who are in conflict. Its 
Diversion Clubs allowed over 1,000 
young people between 13 and 16 
years of age to participate in a drug- 
prevention program. The Entente 
Program, which addresses young 
offenders, welcomed 164 young 
people from 15 different munici- 
palities; while Intersections, which 
responds to the needs of early high- 
school leavers, worked with 58 youth 
in the area and offered a summer 
program for adolescents between 14 
and 17 years of age. The Centre 
works in concert with schools, par- 
ents and anyone else in the youth's 
environment who is willing to help 
him/her through his/her crisis. 


Du Parc YMCA 


The Du Pare YMCA, in cooperation 
with the City of Montreal, has inten- 
sified its involvement as regards 
juvenile delinquency by offering 
sound alternatives to the street; for 
example, it operates a Youth Centre, 
an afterschool program and a pro- 
gram for young offenders. The 
rehabilitation of drug users continues 
to be a serious preoccupation for the 
volunteers and workers who are 
involved with the drug issue. As a 
result, the Du Parc YMCA works to- 
wards the prevention of crime by 
striving to reduce the opportunities 
for youth to commit offenses. 


Hudson Program Centre 


Over 250 volunteers work at the 
Hudson Program Centre. The 
programming it offers includes 
various avant-garde programs and 
services. 


International 
Mutual Support 


In 1989-90 the Montreal YMCA 
supported a dozen different projects 
in El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua 
and Tanzania. On a world scale, 
through the Refugee and Rehabi- 
litation Fund of the World Alliance of 
YMCAs, the Montreal YMCA came 
to the assistance of refugees in 
Sudan, Angola and the Middle-East.

Partners

Montreal 
YMCA 
Statement of 
Operations 
for the Year 
Ended 

May 31, 1990 


Mr. John E. 
Cleghorn at the 
Montreal YMCA 
Youth Enterprise 
Centre 


Report of the 
Chairman of the 
Board of the 
Montreal YMCA 
Foundation, 

Mr. John E. Cleghorn 


Mr. John E. Cleghorn 


It is my pleasure to inform you on the 
activities of the Corporation during 
the past twelve months. 


Sensitization 


In 1989-1990, the members of the 
Board of Directors of the Montreal 
YMCA Foundation personnally met 
with fifty business leaders, in order 
to thank them for their contribution 
to our last Capital Development 
Campaign and keep them up to date 
with the programs and activities of 
the Montreal YMCA. 


Gabrielle and Maurice A. Massé 
Award 


In 1990, the recipient of this presti- 
gious award was a longstanding 
friend of the YMCA, Mr. Frank B. 
Peterson. 


Briefly, Frank first became involved 
with the YMCA in 1936. Over the 
years, he assumed various volunteer 
positions within the organization. In 
particular, he was a member of the 
Metropolitan Board of Directors, 
Founding Chairman of the Verdun- 
Lasalle YMCA and Chairman of the 
1970 Capital Development Campaign 
of the YMCA. Frank Peterson devo- 
ted 50 years of loyal service to our 
Association. 


Foundation Governors 


In October 1989, the Foundation 
appointed Messrs. Brian O.N. Gallery 
and Lucien G. Rolland to the position 
of Governor of the Montreal YMCA 
Foundation. 


Honorary Members 


Mesdames Jean A. Bernard and 
Judith Webster as well as Messrs. 
Raymond Leduc and Norman 
McLeod were elected as Honorary 
Members of the Foundation. 


14

The Finance Committee, which is 
presided over by Mr. Derek 
Hannaford, the Investments Commit- 
tee, chaired by Mr. William Ridley, 
the Needs Analysis Committee 
which is responsible for the analysis 
of requests made for financial assis- 
tance by the YMCA, headed by Mr. 
Victor M. Drury and the Nominating 
Committee whose Chairman is Mr. 
Glenn R. Rourke, complete the admi- 
nistrative structure of the Montreal 
YMCA Foundation and ensures the 
sound operation of the Corporation. 


Report of the 
President of the 
Montreal YMCA 
Foundation, 

Mr. Bernard W. Matte 


The 1989-90 fiscal year marked the 
start of our initial actions in the sec- 
tor of planned giving, in particular 
that of our Insurance Donations 
Program. In 1989, no less than six 
individuals supported the YMCA 
through this program, for a total of 
$564,817. 


Fund-raising programs 


Under the leadership of Mrs. 
Suzanne Aboud, the teams of 
volunteers and staff did a tremen- 
dous job during the annual Sustaining 
Membership Campaign. Further- 
more, a group of fifty people created 
a personal endowment fund during 
the course of the year. Mr. Maurice 
A. Massé is the Chairman of the 
Endowment and Planned Giving 
Program. And, it is with great plea- 
sure that the Foundation inducted 
seven new members into the 
Heritage Club, namely Mr. and Mrs. 
John E. Cleghorn, Mr. and Mrs. David 
Coyle, Mr. and Mrs. John C. Dutton, 
Mr. and Mrs. Thomas S. Gillespie, 
Mr. and Mrs. Ronald C. Loucks, Mr. 
and Mrs. Philip O'Brien, and Mr. and 
Mrs. Frank B. Peterson. 


Special events 


This year, the annual golf tournament 
attracted 140 golfers. Receipts from 
the event, $60,000, were committed 
to community programs of the 
Montreal YMCA to help young 
people who are in conflict with 

the law. 


We wish to extend our sincere 
thanks to our Patrons of Honor for 
their contributions: Air Canada, Bell 
Canada, Saint Lawrence Cement 


Inc., Devencore Real Estate Services 
Ltd., Dominion Textile Inc., Groupe 
La Laurentienne, the Royal Bank of 
Canada, Molson Breweries Ltd., 
Merck Frosst Canada Inc., Pepsi-Cola 
Montreal Ltd., Steinberg Quebec, 
Télé-Direct (Publications) Inc., Sun 
Life Assurance Company of Canada, 
The Gazette, Trizec Equities Limited 
and Ultramar Canada Inc. 


We also wish to thank our four major 
partners, the National Bank of 
Canada, Steinberg Quebec, Télé- 
Direct (Publications) Inc. and St- 
Lawrence Cement Inc., who this year 
sponsored a YMCA cultural benefit 
evening. In fact, the Montreal YMCA 
Foundation bought a supplementary 
performance of Pygmalion, a George 
Bernard Shaw play, which was 
produced by la Compagnie Jean- 
Duceppe inc. The proceeds from 
this event, $45,000, were transferred 
to the International Programs 
Department of the Montreal YMCA. 


Y-A-THON 


The second edition of the Montreal 
YMCA Y-A-Thon was held on Nov- 
ember 19, 1990. Thanks to the 


15 


participation of over 1,400 solicitors 
who performed a physical activity in 
one of our YMCA centres, we suc- 
ceeded in raising $81,000 overall. 
We wish to express our heartfelt 
thanks to Pepsi-Cola Montreal and 
Air Canada as well as to all the com- 
panies that graciously offered us 
their products. 


| also wish to personally thank all the 
employees and volunteers who, once 
again, showed their support for the 
social commitment of the Montreal 
YMCA.
